name: Cheekbone makeup contour/highlight

card.summary: Shading and highlighting to imitate defined cheekbones; reversible and low-risk, with no clinical research behind it.
card.note: Effect is visual and depends on lighting and application.

quick.overview:
Cheekbone contouring uses darker and lighter makeup to suggest more defined cheekbones.

It is a styling technique and has not been studied clinically.
quick.mechanism: Shading under the cheekbone and highlighting on top change the perceived depth and shape of the cheek through light and shadow.
quick.risks: Makeup carries the usual risks of skin irritation or allergic reaction with some products. The effect is temporary and washes off.

lead: Cheekbone contouring and highlighting is a makeup technique that creates the look of higher, sharper cheekbones. A shade one or two tones darker than the skin goes in the hollow beneath the cheekbone, and a lighter or shimmery highlighter goes on the raised top of the bone, so that the shadow recedes and the highlight catches light [1]. It lets people change how their face reads in photos and in person without surgery, and it washes off the same day.

The method sits within the broader practice of contouring, which also shades the sides of the nose, the temples and the jawline. Wikipedia traces it from theatre makeup and 1930s Hollywood work by Max Factor through Kevyn Aucoin's 2000 book Face Forward to the intense, widely shared looks of the 2010s popularised by Kim Kardashian's makeup artists [1].

In appearance communities it is discussed as a reversible way to add facial definition, for people who want more prominent cheekbones, a leaner midface or a stronger photographic presence. No clinical research has measured how contour makeup changes perceived attractiveness.

chain: Darker shade under the cheekbone, lighter shade on top
Shadow and highlight change how the cheek reflects light
Cheekbones look higher and the midface looks more defined
angle.text: Contour and highlight change how light falls across the cheek, so the cheekbone looks more prominent and the face looks leaner or more sculpted. The effect depends on shade match, blending and lighting, and it lasts until the makeup is removed.

Max Factor (1930s), Kevyn Aucoin (1990s-2000), social media (2010s)

paras: Wikipedia describes contouring as using cosmetics to define and sculpt facial structure: a darker tone in hollows creates shadow, and a lighter highlighter on prominent areas draws attention forward. For cheekbones, the dark shade goes below the bone and the highlight sits on the raised area [1].

Powder contour products are usually sold in palettes with light and dark shades, while cream products give a more emphasised look [1]. Shadow tends to recede and light tends to advance, which is why placement along the hollow and on the bone changes how the cheek appears, and why the effect varies with lighting and camera angle.

Wikipedia records that Elizabethan actors used chalk and soot so audiences could read expressions, and that greasepaint later replaced soot under electric stage lights [1]. In the 1930s Max Factor Sr. added shading so faces would not look flat on screen, and in 1945 he published a tutorial on contouring for different face shapes [1].

Makeup artist Kevyn Aucoin's 2000 book Face Forward is credited with introducing contouring to the general public, and in the 2010s Kim Kardashian and other makeup artists made the technique more intense and mainstream while affordable brands began selling contour and strobing products [1]. Drag performers also use contouring to emphasise or soften features [1].

The apparent shape of the cheek reflects both the skeleton and the soft tissue over it. Surgical anatomy papers describe the midcheek as built from lid-cheek, malar and nasolabial segments over the midcheek skeleton [2], and describe age-related changes in separate superficial and deep fat compartments [3]. Those papers concern surgery and injectables rather than makeup, but they describe the structures that contour and highlight imitate: a prominent malar bone with a hollow beneath it.

Contouring is mainly discussed in style and grooming circles as a non-surgical, low-cost option for people who want stronger cheekbones, alongside facial-fat reduction, fillers and implants for those who prefer lasting changes. Users on forums describe it as a way to test how a more defined midface would look before committing to a procedure.
No studies found. Anatomy literature describes the cheek but does not examine contour makeup.

timeline.event: Max Factor Sr. adds shading so faces do not look flat on film [1].
